kept.title: Insufficient Header Stripping on Cross-Domain Redirects
kept.description: The logic in index.js:486-491 attempts to strip sensitive headers when redirecting to a different domain, but the check for `isSubdomain` can be bypassed by crafty host naming, potentially leaking Authorization or Cookie headers to malicious third-party servers.
steps_to_exploit: User initiates a request with Authorization headers to a trusted domain.
Attacker controls a redirect response pointing to a maliciously named subdomain or a host that suffix-matches.
The library fails the security check in index.js:489.
The library forwards the Authorization header to the attacker-controlled server.
kept.impact: Exposure of sensitive authentication tokens and cookies to unauthorized third-party domains.

kept.title: Open Redirection via User-Supplied Input
kept.description: The library automatically follows Location headers without restricting the target domain, effectively acting as an open redirector for any URL provided to it.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker provides a malicious URL to the application using this library.
The server performs a request to a URL controlled by the attacker.
The attacker's server returns a 302 Redirect to a high-value or phishing target.
The library automatically redirects the client to the victim's phishing page.
kept.impact: Facilitates phishing attacks and server-side request forgery (SSRF).

kept.title: SSRF via Unrestricted Protocol Redirection
kept.description: The library allows upgrading/changing protocols during redirection (e.g., from HTTP to HTTPS or potentially others), which can be abused to probe internal network services.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker triggers an HTTP request to an internal-only IP address.
The server responds with a 302 redirecting to a different port or internal loopback address.
The library follows the redirect to the internal service.
The response from the internal service might be leaked or used to confirm internal network structure.
kept.impact: Server-Side Request Forgery enabling internal network reconnaissance.

kept.title: Unbounded Redirection Recursion
kept.description: The `maxRedirects` default is 21, which is high enough to allow resource exhaustion attacks or to cause excessive load on external systems during a redirect loop.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker creates a sequence of 21 redirects.
The client library processes all 21 requests.
Attacker repeats this process across multiple parallel connections to consume server socket resources.
kept.impact: Denial of service through resource consumption and potential latency amplification.

kept.title: Large Body Accumulation in Memory
kept.description: The library buffers the entire request body to potentially re-send it on subsequent redirects, capped at 10MB by default, which can lead to memory exhaustion.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker sends a POST request with a large body (close to 10MB).
Attacker ensures the server returns a redirect.
The library clones the large body into memory for the next request.
Simultaneously executing many such requests leads to heap exhaustion.
kept.impact: Memory exhaustion leading to Node.js process crash (Denial of Service).

kept.title: Host Header Injection/Confusion
kept.description: The library manually manages the Host header and allows it to be modified or re-set during redirects, leading to potential Host header poisoning.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker provides a request with a specific Host header.
The library's `_sanitizeOptions` modifies the Host logic.
The redirect process incorrectly carries over headers to the target, allowing the attacker to spoof the Host for virtual-hosting-based applications.
kept.impact: Cache poisoning and bypass of virtual host security constraints.

kept.title: Insecure `beforeRedirect` Callback Usage
kept.description: The `beforeRedirect` hook allows users to mutate `options` and `headers` without providing a safe way to validate or sanitize the target, leading to potential security bypasses in downstream application logic.
steps_to_exploit: Application uses `beforeRedirect` to inject custom headers.
User-provided input inside the request is used to inform the `beforeRedirect` logic.
Attacker manipulates input to set arbitrary sensitive headers (e.g., X-Forwarded-For) via the callback.
kept.impact: Security logic bypasses and potential header injection.

kept.title: Missing Validation of Protocol Schemes
kept.description: The library relies on `nativeProtocols` map but doesn't strictly validate that the redirected URL protocol matches an allowed set, potentially allowing usage of unintended protocols like `file://` or `gopher://` if the environment supports them.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker provides a redirect Location header with a non-HTTP scheme.
The internal `_performRequest` checks if the protocol exists in `nativeProtocols`.
If the environment or runtime monkey-patches `https` with other modules, arbitrary protocol execution is possible.

kept.title: Regex Injection in Header Filter
kept.description: The `sensitiveHeaders` filter is constructed using `new RegExp`, and while there is an `escapeRegex` function, any misconfiguration or future changes to `sensitiveHeaders` could lead to regex injection.
steps_to_exploit: An attacker influences the contents of `sensitiveHeaders` if exposed through configuration.
The library constructs a regex from user-controlled strings.
The regex logic fails to safely block headers.

kept.title: Possible Integer Overflow in Body Length Calculation
kept.description: The `_requestBodyLength` calculation is a simple arithmetic addition. While unlikely in JS due to IEEE 754, in specific custom implementations, this could lead to logic bypasses if `maxBodyLength` is manipulated to be very large.
steps_to_exploit: Application allows setting an extremely high `maxBodyLength`.
Attacker sends fragmented data to cause integer wrapping during cumulative additions.
The limit check is bypassed.
kept.impact: Bypass of body size limits leading to DoS.

kept.title: Use of `Object.create(null)` for Event Handlers
kept.description: While generally safe, if the library were to allow event handler modification via user input, this could lead to prototype pollution in other areas of the application.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker finds a way to pass objects into the initialization of `RedirectableRequest`.
The library uses `Object.create(null)` for event handlers, but other parts of the code use plain objects.
Prototype pollution occurs through object merging.
kept.impact: Application instability and potential security control bypasses.

kept.title: Improper Cleanup on Timeout Events
kept.description: The `clearTimer` function removes listeners, but there is a risk of race conditions where listeners might be re-added or triggered after the object is destroyed.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker triggers a timeout concurrently with an error.
The cleanup function executes, but the event loop might have already queued the timeout callback.
Zombie timers trigger unintended logic.

kept.title: Insecure Handling of `auth` URL field
kept.description: The `preservedUrlFields` includes `auth`, which carries credentials. The code does not explicitly scrub the `auth` field when redirecting to a different domain, potentially sending credentials to a malicious site.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker provides a URL with embedded basic auth.
The library redirects to a different origin.
The `spreadUrlObject` copies the `auth` field to the new request options.
The credentials are sent to the attacker-controlled origin.

kept.title: Error Disclosure in CustomError
kept.description: The `CustomError` constructor appends `this.cause.message` to the error message, potentially leaking internal server details or file system paths if an internal error occurs during request processing.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker sends a request that triggers an internal error (e.g., invalid URL, protocol error).
The library captures the native error and wraps it.
The response sent to the client includes the stack trace or descriptive error internal to the library.
kept.impact: Information disclosure of internal application state.

kept.title: Lack of Explicit `content-length` stripping on Redirects
kept.description: When method is changed to GET, the library drops content-related headers but does not explicitly ensure `content-length` is zeroed out or removed for all scenarios, potentially causing desync issues.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker initiates a POST request.
The redirect logic switches the method to GET.
The `content-length` header from the original POST remains in the headers object.
A proxy or downstream server might misinterpret the subsequent GET request due to the presence of a length header.
